---
title: "Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub"
---

One member of the group does this once, while the others watch. Then everyone
does it again alone, with a throwaway project, because you only learn it by
doing it.

Every command on this page has been run for real; the outputs shown are the
actual outputs.

## 1. Make an RStudio Project

In RStudio: **File → New Project → New Directory → New Project**.

- Directory name: `penguin-clinic`
- Create as a subdirectory of: somewhere sensible, e.g. `~/projects`
- Leave "Create a git repository" **unchecked** — we will do it deliberately

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not put your project in Dropbox, OneDrive or iCloud

A sync client and git both want to manage the same files, and the sync client
can corrupt git's internal bookkeeping by writing into `.git` at the wrong
moment. More importantly: **GitHub is now your sharing mechanism.** Putting a
git project in a sync folder is doing the same job twice, badly.

Use `~/projects/` or `Documents/projects/` — anywhere that is not synced.
:::

Why a Project and not just a folder? Because `.Rproj` fixes your working
directory. Every path in your code becomes relative to the project root, so
`read.csv("data/clinic_visits.csv")` works on your teammate's laptop too. This
is a precondition for collaboration, not a nicety.

## 2. Open the project folder in Claude Code

Open Claude Code and point it at the project folder you just made. It needs to
be *in* the project, otherwise it will put files in the wrong place.

## 3. Build the project skeleton

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Set up this R project for group work: an `R/` folder with three analysis
> scripts, a `data-raw/` script that simulates a small dataset, a `data/`
> folder, and a `report.qmd` that sources the scripts. Also write a README
> saying who owns which file.
:::

The structure we are aiming at:

``` text
penguin-clinic/
├── penguin-clinic.Rproj
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── data-raw/00-simulate-data.R   # makes the data, so provenance is in the repo
├── data/clinic_visits.csv        # 4 KB, simulated
├── R/01-clean.R                  # student A owns
├── R/02-describe.R               # student B owns
├── R/03-model.R                  # student C owns
└── report.qmd                    # shared; conflicts live here
```

**Check it works before going near git.** A broken project in version control
is still broken.

```bash
Rscript -e 'source("R/01-clean.R"); print(nrow(load_visits()))'
```

## 4. Start the repository and write a `.gitignore`

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Make this a git repository with `main` as the default branch, and write a
> `.gitignore` suitable for an R and Quarto project. Keep the small simulated
> CSV in version control but exclude RStudio session state, rendered output
> and anything that looks like a secret.
:::

```bash
git init -b main
```

The `.gitignore` is the one file worth understanding, because the mistakes it
prevents are the expensive ones:

``` text
# RStudio session junk — machine-specific, never useful to anyone else
.Rproj.user/
.Rhistory
.RData

# secrets: NEVER commit these
.Renviron
.env

# rendered output — commit the source, not the result
report.html
report_files/
/_site/
/.quarto/

# OS noise
.DS_Store
```

::: {.callout-important}
## "Never commit data" is wrong advice

You will hear it anyway. The real criterion is:

| Commit it | Do not commit it |
|---|---|
| Small (< ~1 MB) | Large — git stores every version forever |
| Simulated or public | Personal, identifiable, or under a data agreement |
| Needed to run the code | Re-derivable from something else in the repo |

Our 4 KB simulated CSV is committed on purpose: without it, nobody can run
your code. A real patient export would be excluded, and the README would say
where to get it.

And the hard part: **git never forgets.** If you commit a file with patient
data or an API key and then delete it, it is still in the history and still
on GitHub. Removing it properly is difficult and you must assume the secret is
burned. So get `.gitignore` right *before* the first commit.
:::

## 5. First commit

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Show me what would be committed, then commit it with a message explaining
> what this project is.
:::

```bash
git status --short          # ?? means untracked
git add -A
git status --short          # A  means staged
git commit -m "Set up project skeleton for the group analysis"
```

Confirm the `.gitignore` actually worked:

```bash
git status --ignored --short | grep '^!!'
```

Real output from this project:

``` text
!! report.html
!! report_files/
```

That is `.gitignore` doing its job. If you see `!! data/patient_export.csv`,
good. If you see it staged with `A `, stop and fix it.

## 6. Create the GitHub repository and push

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Create a public GitHub repository called penguin-clinic from this folder and
> push main to it.
:::

```bash
gh repo create penguin-clinic --public --source=. --remote=origin --push
```

Real output:

``` text
https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic
To https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic.git
 * [new branch]      HEAD -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
```

That one command did three things worth naming:

1. created the repository on GitHub
2. added it to your local repo under the name **`origin`** — that word just
   means "the GitHub copy"
3. pushed `main` and set it to *track* `origin/main`, so from now on plain
   `git push` and `git pull` know where to go

Open the URL. Your files are there. Check that the ignored ones are **not**.

## 7. The loop you will now repeat forever

Change something in RStudio → commit → push → refresh the browser.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Commit and push this change, with a message explaining why I did it.
:::

Watch RStudio's **Git pane** (top right, appears after you reopen the project)
while you do it. It is the window through which you see the four places from
[Part 1](01-concepts.qmd):

- files appear with `?` when untracked, `M` when modified
- checkboxes are the **staging area**
- *Commit* moves them into your **local history**
- the **↑ / ↓ arrows** show how many commits you are ahead of / behind GitHub

::: {.callout-note}
## Look at the arrows every time you sit down

`↓ 2` means your teammates have pushed twice and you do not have their work
yet. **Pull before you start.** That one habit prevents most conflicts.
:::

## 8. Add your teammates

On GitHub: **Settings → Collaborators → Add people**. They need to accept the
invitation by email before they can push.

```bash
gh repo view --web    # opens the repo in your browser
```
